---
title: "Attributes and Custom Procedural Macros"
description: "One Rust language concept taught with one short runnable example and a precise explanation."
---

## The question

**Can Rust define something like Java's `@MyAnnotation`?**

The closest syntax is an attribute such as `#[derive(Debug)]` or a custom `#[my_attribute]`. But Rust attributes are mainly **compile-time metadata / transformations**, not Java-style runtime-reflection objects.

## The rule to remember

Built-in and derive attributes can be used in one file. Defining a new attribute macro requires a separate **proc-macro crate**; the demonstration below is intentionally the smallest truthful example.

## The smallest complete example

Paste into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`. The [Rust examples page](examples/index.qmd) describes how to check all snippets automatically.

~~~rust
#[derive(Debug)]
struct User { id: u32 }
fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", User { id: 7 }); // User { id: 7 }
}
~~~

**Follow the state:** `#[derive(Debug)]` asks an existing derive macro to generate an implementation of `Debug` for `User`. The `{:?}` formatter can then display the struct. `#[cfg(test)]` controls conditional compilation; not every attribute generates a trait implementation.

## Important limitation

A custom attribute macro receives token streams and returns token streams. It is not a no-code annotation tag that Rust reflects upon at runtime. Production procedural macros should parse syntax carefully (often with `syn`/`quote`) and provide diagnostics; the minimal lab purposely uses fixed output without dependencies.
